text:
A pace plan treats the body as a fixed engine, but the body also has a fuel tank. A trained runner stores roughly 400 to 500 grams of glycogen in the muscles and liver, which covers about 2,000 calories. Marathon pace burns close to 100 calories per mile, so that reserve runs out somewhere near mile 20.

After that, the body has to rely on fat oxidation, which delivers ATP more slowly. A runner who banked a few seconds early, on a cool, flat first half, now finds the account overdrawn. Splits that looked sustainable at mile 12 demand power the fuel system cannot release. Heat, dehydration (a loss of two percent of body mass), and eccentric quad damage make the deficit worse. Then the wall arrives.

To prevent it, run negative splits, take in 60 to 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour, and do long runs that train your body to burn fat before race day.
